title: This Custom 1979 Chevy Van Isn’t a Throwback. It’s a Survivor.

body_markdown:
While visiting automotive artist Randy Grubb to photograph[his amazing McLaren M6GT build](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/automotive-artist-pieced-together-stunning-mclaren-m6gt/) , we scoped out photo locations in his 1979 Chevy van. Aside from the[Grand National Truck Show](https://www.hagerty.com/media/events/8-great-chevys-from-the-first-ever-grand-national-truck-show/) , which gathers custom vans from Southern California, a van with custom paint and upholstery is a bit of a rare sight, so we made sure to capture photos of Randy’s other mid-engine vehicle to share with you. We also asked Randy to share a bit about how he became its steward.


Custom vans in the ’70s and ’80s were all about personalized interiors. Randy’s features swiveling front seats, wood paneling, and a rear seat that folds into a bed.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Randy spotted the vintage custom for sale on Facebook Marketplace. He was initially attracted by the van’s inherent utility and interior room. Amazingly, its custom touches had survived intact. Still, he was hoping for an earlier model, one with round headlights, and he was leery of buying a van with a sunroof.


He knew that the roof was prone to rust even if it hadn’t been cut, so he kept his eyes open. “I’m looking at these other vans, and they’re rusty, crusty,” said Randy. “And I hate rust, man. I mean, just hate it.” Then he thought back to the first van he looked at, this one. It didn’t have any rust, he realized. The other small issues were things he could live with.


He talked himself back into the original van, noting that a grille swap would be a simple bit of wrenching. After some more thought, the sunroof didn’t seem like a deal-killer.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The more he thought about the van, the more this well-kept custom appealed to him. Randy appreciated that this was a Bonanza, which meant it had nicer trim and some added details like a padded doghouse over the engine. Even better, the van was never used as a work vehicle. It had always been stored inside, and the drip rails, where many vans rust due to shrinking and cracking seam sealer, were in good shape, even though they were starting to show some weathering. After striking a deal, he took delivery of the van and started to make it his own.


Randy installed air conditioning from another van. It required cutting the dash to fit vents, but with a factory bezel it looks just as it would if it were originally equipped.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Randy got in touch with the previous owner, the one who had sold it to the person from whom Randy bought it. He’s the one who installed the 330-hp 350 crate engine, rebuilt the rear axle with a 3.71:1 Positraction differential, upgraded to[Wilwood brakes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-wilwood-turns-aluminum-chunks-into-brake-calipers/) , and treated the suspension to a rebuild with polyurethane bushings. After learning about all of the care and effort that had gone into the van, Randy was even more sure that he’d made the right call.


The Wilwood brakes are just visible through the aluminum five-spoke wheels.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


What was most remarkable about the van was how well preserved it was, with its 45-year-old upholstery remarkably intact.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Randy has made a few additions to the inside to personalize the van. **** He found a donor van and swapped in factory air conditioning, right down to the correct bezel. The biggest visual change is the earlier grille, with round headlights—a must for Randy. He also added a 700-R4 in place of the Turbo 350 automatic. The 3.73:1 gears make the van quite peppy, and now that it has overdrive, it’s also a solid road tripper. Other than those changes, much of the van remains as it was, with all its customized touches, which is how Randy likes it.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


“The pinstriping was done in ’81 by Paul Mackey, who was one of Portland’s iconic pinstripers from the day,” said Randy. Almost all of the vintage pinstriping was intact, and Randy very carefully touched it up where needed.


The van shows nicely, and the swivel seats turn it into a great place to hang out at a car show. Most won’t even notice the few spots where the van is showing its age: “If you stand up there and grab onto the roof rail, you can see my roof has seen better days,” Randy said. While he considered sealing the small patch of surface rust with a patina preserver, he opted instead for an epoxy primer. “The rusty top really isn’t working for me.”


The van has served Randy well, as the newly found long-distance capability offered by the overdrive transmission has really expanded its cruising radius, allowing it to roll up at more car shows. Thanks to a new caretaker who handles all of the issues that come up on a 45-year-old custom, it has lots more car shows in its future, with fewer blemishes each time.


“I want something a little more finished, so we’ll work in that direction,” said Randy. We can’t wait to see it.
